title: 3  Bell’s Theorem
text:
3.1 Locality and causality assumptions
Bell’s theorem has an untidy history. It is even debatable whether it merits being called a theorem. However, it is extremely important, as shown below, and ought to be shaped into the form of a theorem.
The proof is in two parts, as in Myrvold et al. (2020):
This will show a conflict between a statistical analysis of possible experiments that assumes a locality concept called Bell locality (BL), and textbook quantum mechanics (QM). Further discussion is then devoted to the challenge of deciding experimentally between BL and QM.
The framework is a generalisation of the one used in Bell (1964). Bell’s 1964 derivation assumed an experiment involving perfect anticorrelation of the results of aligned Stern-Gerlach experiments on a pair of entangled spin-\(\frac{1}{2}\) particles. This is not realistic, and experimental tests need this assumption to be relaxed because of the practical difficulties of maintaining quantum coherence and guaranteeing spacelike separation of the measurements. An experimental setup with polarised photons is more appropriate. Papers that took the steps from Bell’s 1964 demonstration to an experimentally testable form include John F. Clauser et al. (1969), Bell (1971), Clauser and Horne (1974), Aspect (1983) and Mermin (1986).
The initial part of the proof will use a framework describing the general experimental setup and the assumptions sufficient to ensure satisfaction of the Bell inequalities. The second part will show that quantum mechanics predicts violations of the inequalities. The conceptual framework postulates an ensemble of configurations of two correlated subsystems, with each entangled system labelled 1 and 2. Each entangled system is characterised by a configuration state \(z\) that contains the entirety of its properties, including the properties of the individual sub-systems and any correlations between them. The state \(z\) is taken to be a complete specification of the properties of the configuration at the moment of generation and future evolution, other than future experimental decisions.
The state space \(Z\) is the totality of all states \(z\), and it is assumed that the subsets of \(Z\) are measurable subsets, forming a measurable space to which probabilistic considerations may be applied. The probability distribution over \(Z\) is denoted by \(\delta\). In addition, it is assumed that the mode of generation of the pairs establishes a probability distribution \(p\) that is independent of the histories of each of the two systems after they separate. Temporal evolution of the properties of the two systems after separation is possible, but it is assumed that the state \(z\) sets the probabilities for subsequent events (including any temporal evolution), and therefore the probabilities for outcomes of experiments to be performed on the sub-systems separately.
Different experiments may be performed on each subsystem. Use \(a \in \mathcal{A}\) as variables ranging over possible experiment settings \(\mathcal{A}\) on subsystem 1, and \(b \in \mathcal{B}\) as variables ranging over experiment settings \(\mathcal{B}\) on subsystem 2. It is not assumed that these parameters capture the complete state of the experimental apparatus, which might have a range of microstates corresponding to each experimental setting; consider them as labels. The following assumption concerns experimental procedures and the independence of the preparation of the entangled system from the choice of experiments to be performed.
The results of an experiment with setting \(a\) on subsystem 1 are labelled by a real parameter \(s\), taking values from a discrete set \(S_a\) of real numbers in the interval \([-1,1]\). Equivalently, the result of an experiment on subsystem 2 is labelled by a parameter \(\tau\), taking values from a discrete set \(T_b\) in \([-1,1]\). The sets of possible outcomes depend on the choice of experimental settings. The restriction of the outcome labels to the interval \([-1,1]\) is a choice made only for convenience. It is essentially a measurement calibration, and it is important that the calibration be consistent across all experiments. The restriction to discrete outcome sets is not essential, but it is convenient for the proof of the Bell inequalities.
It is assumed that, for each pair of settings \(a,b\), and every \(z \in Z\), there is a probability function \(p_{a,b}(s,\tau \mid z)\), which obviously sums to unity over all \(s \in S_a\) and \(\tau \in T_b\). These probabilities are used to define marginal probabilities:
\[ p^1_{a,b}(s \mid z) \equiv \sum_{\tau \in T_b} p_{a,b}(s,\tau \mid z),  \tag{3.1}\]
\[ p^2_{a,b}(\tau \mid z) \equiv \sum_{s \in S_a} p_{a,b}(s,\tau \mid z),  \tag{3.2}\]
Define \(A_z(a,b)\) and \(B_z(a,b)\) as the expectation values, for complete state \(z\), of the outcomes of experiments on subsystems 1 and 2, respectively, when the settings are \(a,b\).
\[A_z(a,b) \equiv \sum_{s \in S_a} s \, p^1_{a,b}(s \mid z) \tag{3.3}\]
\[B_z(a,b) \equiv \sum_{\tau \in T_b} \tau \, p^2_{a,b}(\tau \mid z) \tag{3.4}\]
Now define the expectation value of the product \(s \cdot \tau\) of outcomes:
\[E_z(a,b) \equiv \sum_{s \in S_a,\, \tau \in T_b} (s \cdot \tau)\,p_{a,b}(s,\tau\mid z). \tag{3.5}\]
Bell-type inequalities follow from considerations of locality and causality that have been called factorisability or Bell locality (BL). This is formulated as the following factorisation condition on the response probability distribution of outcomes, conditional on the complete state \(z\) of the configuration.
(BL) For any \(a,b,z\), there exist probability functions \(p^1_a(s \mid z)\) and \(p^2_b(\tau \mid z)\) such that
\[
p_{a,b}(s,\tau \mid z) = p^1_a(s \mid z)\,p^2_b(\tau \mid z).
\]
Note that, even though the probability factors into independent subsystem-1 and subsystem-2 probabilities conditional on the total system state \(z\), the outcome in subsystem 1 does not depend on the setting of the experiment in subsystem 2, and vice versa. The condition (BL) is a consequence of the conjunction of two conditions, which have been called parameter independence and outcome independence (see Section 3.1, below).
If the factorisability condition (BL) is satisfied, then \(A_z(a,b)=A_z(a)\) and \(B_z(a,b)=B_z(b)\), so
\[E_z(a,b) = A_z(a) B_z(b). \tag{3.6}\]
The above definitions are valid for experiments with any number of discrete outcomes. The simplest case is that in which each experiment has only two distinct outcomes, labelled by \(\pm 1\).
To derive the inequalities, at least two separate experimental settings per subsystem must be considered, \(a,a',b,b'\). Now consider the quantities
\[S_z(a,a',b,b') = \lvert E_z(a,b) + E_z(a,b') \rvert + \lvert E_z(a',b) - E_z(a',b') \rvert. \tag{3.7}\]
Now introduce a quantity related to \(S_z(a,a',b,b')\), namely \(S_\delta\), where the expectation values in Equation 3.7 are averaged over \(\delta\), the distribution over states \(z \in Z\).
\[ S_\delta(a,a',b,b') = \lvert\langle E_z(a,b) \rangle_\delta + \langle E_z(a,b') \rangle_\delta\rvert\] \[ + \lvert\langle E_z(a',b) \rangle_\delta - \langle E_z(a',b') \rangle_\delta\rvert.  \tag{3.8}\]
Note that, in taking the expectation values of the quantities appearing on the right-hand side of this definition with respect to the same distribution \(\delta\), invoking the Measurement Independence Assumption. Under this assumption and the BL condition, the following is proved in J. F. Clauser et al. (1969).:
Bell’s theorem — part 1: For \(S_\delta(a,a',b,b')\) given by Equation 3.8, the following inequality holds:
\[\tag{BT1} S_\delta(a,a',b,b') \leq 2.\]
This is known as the CHSH (Clauser–Horne–Shimony–Holt) inequality.
Proof
From Equation 3.7
\[ \langle S_z(a,a',b,b') \rangle_\delta = \langle \lvert E_z(a,b) + E_z(a,b') \rvert \rangle_\delta + \langle \lvert E_z(a',b) - E_z(a',b') \rvert \rangle_\delta. \]
Since the absolute value of the average of any random variable cannot be greater than the average of its absolute value, it is clear that
\[S_\delta(a,a',b,b') \leq \langle S_z(a,a',b,b') \rangle_\delta. \tag{3.9}\]
If BL is satisfied, then, using Equation 3.5 and the fact that \(A_z(a)\) and \(A_z(a')\) lie in the interval \([-1,1]\),
\[ S_z(a,a',b,b')  \tag{3.10}\]
\[= \lvert A_z(a)(B_z(b) + B_z(b'))\rvert + \lvert A_z(a')(B_z(b) - B_z(b'))\rvert\]
\[\leq \lvert B_z(b) + B_z(b') \rvert + \lvert B_z(b) - B_z(b')\rvert. \]
It is easy to check that
\[\lvert B_z(b) + B_z(b') \rvert + \lvert B_z(b) - B_z(b') \rvert = 2\max(\lvert B_z(b) \rvert,\,\lvert B_z(b')\rvert).\]
Since \(B_z(b)\) and \(B_z(b')\) also lie in the interval \([-1,1]\), from the previous step, for every \(z\),
\[S_z(a,a',b,b') \leq 2. \tag{3.11}\]
Since this bound holds for every value of \(z\), it must also hold for the expectation value of \(S_z\).
\[\langle S_z(a,a',b,b')\rangle_\delta \leq 2. \tag{3.12}\]
This, together with Equation 3.9, yields the CHSH inequality and completes the proof of BT1. \(\square\)
The final step of the proof of our Bell theorem is to show that a system described by a quantum mechanical state violates BT1, the CHSH inequality.
Bell’s theorem — part 2: There is a quantum mechanical state and a set of experiments for which the CHSH inequality is violated.
\[\tag{BT2} \langle S_z(a,a',b,b')\rangle_\delta \nleq 2.\]
The set of experiments used to test the CHSH inequality will be referred to as CHSH experiments. Here, consider one example involving polarisation-entangled photons, Figure 3.1.
Consider a pair of photons 1 and 2 propagating in the \(\zeta\)-direction. Let \(\phi_{\chi}\) and \(\phi_{\upsilon}\) represent states in which photon \(j\) (\(j=1,2\)) is linearly polarised in the \(\chi\)- and \(\upsilon\)-directions, respectively. Neglecting the part of the state that describes movement in the \(\zeta\)-direction, consider the following part of the state vector that describes the polarisation of the photons:
\[\Phi = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\phi_{\chi,1} \otimes \phi_{\chi, 2} + \phi_{\upsilon, 1} \otimes\phi_{\upsilon, 2} \right), \tag{3.13}\]
which is invariant under rotation of the \(\chi\) and \(\upsilon\) axes in the plane perpendicular to \(\zeta\). The total quantum state of the pair of photons 1 and 2 is invariant under exchange of the two photons, as required by the fact that photons are integral-spin particles. Suppose now that photons 1 and 2 impinge respectively on the faces of birefringent crystal polarisation analyzers I and II, with the entrance face of each analyzer perpendicular to \(\zeta\). Each analyzer has the property of separating light incident upon its face into two outgoing non-parallel rays, the ordinary ray and the extraordinary ray. The transmission axis of the analyzer is a direction with the property that a photon polarised along it will emerge in the ordinary ray (with certainty if the crystals are assumed to be ideal), while a photon polarised in a direction perpendicular to \(\zeta\) and to the transmission axis will emerge in the extraordinary ray. See Figure 3.1 for a schematic of the experimental setup.
Photon pairs are emitted from the source, each pair quantum mechanically described by \(\Phi\) of Equation 3.13. I and II are polarisation analyzers, with outcomes \(s=1\) and \(\tau=1\) designating emergence in the ordinary ray, while \(s=-1\) and \(\tau=-1\) designate emergence in the extraordinary ray. The crystals are also idealised by assuming that no incident photon is absorbed.
The expectation value, in state \(\Phi\), of the product of \(s\) and \(\tau\), is
\[E_{\Phi}(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}) =\cos^2 (\theta_{\mathbf{a} \mathbf{b}}) - \sin^2 (\theta_{\mathbf{a} \mathbf{b}}) \tag{3.14}\]
\[= \cos(2\theta_{\mathbf{a} \mathbf{b}}).\]
The details are calculated in Section 3.2, below.
Here \(\theta_{\mathbf{a} \mathbf{b}} = \alpha-\beta\) is the angle between the transmission axes of the two analyzers. The expectation value \(E_{\Phi}(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})\) is a correlation function, and it is a function of the angle between the transmission axes of the two analyzers. The correlation function is maximal when the transmission axes are aligned, and minimal when they are perpendicular.
An important insight of Bell’s was that it is important to consider the less-than-perfect correlations obtained when the device axes are not aligned. Bell’s theorem shows that no model satisfying the condition BL can reproduce the quantum correlations for all angles. This can be seen by considering the quantum predictions (Equation 3.13, Equation 3.14) and plugging them into the expression for \(S\). For the case of polarisation-entangled photons
\[S_{\Phi}(\theta) = \lvert 2 \cos(2\theta)\rvert + \lvert \cos(2\theta) - \cos(6\theta) \rvert. \tag{3.15}\]
This takes on its maximum at \(\theta = \pi/8\).
\[S_{\Phi}(\pi/8) = 2\sqrt{2} \approx 2.828. \tag{3.16}\]
The key condition giving rise to the Bell inequality (BT1) is the factorisability condition (BL). This condition is motivated by considerations of locality and causality. It is also a purely mathematical relationship between probabilities. For the proof, it is only necessary to find one system described by a quantum state and a set of experiments for which the CHSH inequality is violated. However, for experimental tests it is important to understand the physical assumptions that motivate the condition (BL) and ensure that these are met. In this section these assumptions are discussed.

title: 3  Bell’s Theorem
text:
3.1.1 Bell’s Principle of Local Causality
Bell’s Principle of Local Causality has evolved since the publication of Bell (1964). The details of this evolution are not important here, but rather the core idea is that the result of a measurement on one system be independent of the setting of a distant measurement, provided the two measurements were not coordinated in their joint past.
In his final contribution (Bell and Aspect (2004)), Bell derives the factorisability condition (BL) from the Principle of Local Causality. He bases his analysis on the following:

relativity prohibits superluminal causation;
the cause-effect relation is asymmetric in time, with causes temporally preceding their effects;
in a relativistic spacetime, events at spacelike separation are taken to have no temporal order.

Bell’s final statement of the Principle of Local Causality is as follows (see Figure 3.2):

Principle of Local Causality (PLC): A theory will be said to be locally causal if the probabilities attached to values of local beables in a spacetime region 1 are unaltered by specification of values of local beables in a spacelike separated region 2, when what happens in the backward light cone of 1 is already sufficiently specified, for example by a full specification of local beables in a spacetime region 3.







Figure 3.2: Principle of Local Causality



Bell’s term beable means any element of a physical theory that is taken to correspond to something physically real; therefore a beable is an entity in the Real Sphere as described in Critical ontology and layers of reality, and local beables pertaining to a spacetime region are those contained within that region. The term was, of course, introduced to generalise beyond the term observable in textbook QM.
Note that the preparation state \(z\) is a complete specification of the properties of the entangled system at the moment of generation, and hence is in the backward light cone of both region 1 and region 2.
The formulation of the local causality condition is motivated by Bell (1976) with the remark,

Now my intuitive notion of local causality is that events in spacetime region 2 should not be “causes” of events in spacelike separated region 1, and vice versa. But this does not mean that the two sets of events should be uncorrelated, for they could have common causes in the overlap of their backward light cones.

The system state \(z\) is a common cause of correlations between the two subsystems. Correlations between two variables that are not in a cause-effect relation to each other can be explained by some common cause.
Bell then proceeds to formulate the condition of local causality, which is that a full specification of beables in the overlap of the backward light cones of the spacetime regions 1 and 2 should screen off correlations between them. Implicit in this is that correlations between two variables be susceptible to causal explanation, either via a causal connection between the variables, or via a common cause.
The Principle of Local Causality follows from the conjunction of three assumptions, all of which were explicitly formulated by Bell:

(Temporal Asymmetry of Causality) Any cause of an event lies in its temporal past, and not in its temporal future.
(Lorentz Invariance) The relation of temporal precedence is invariant under Lorentz boosts.
Common cause.



3.1.2 Parameter independence and outcome independence
The condition BL of factorisability is the application, to the particular setup of CHSH experiments, of Bell’s Principle of Local Causality. As shown, it can be thought of as the conjunction of the condition of causal locality and the common-cause principle. In this subsection those conditions are applied to the setup of CHSH experiments.
On the assumption that the experimental settings can be treated as free variables, whose choice of setting on one wing is made at spacelike separation from the experiment on the other, a dependence of the probability of the outcome of one experiment on the setting of the other would seem straightforwardly to be an instance of a nonlocal causal influence. The condition that this not occur can be formulated as follows.
(PI) For all parameter settings \(a\), \(a'\), \(b\), \(b'\), all \(z\), and all \(s \in S_a\) and \(\tau \in T_b\),
\[p^1_{a,b}(s \mid z) = p^1_{a,b'}(s \mid z); \tag{3.17}\]
\[p^2_{a,b}(\tau \mid z) = p^2_{a',b}(\tau \mid z). \tag{3.18}\]
This is the condition that has come to be known as parameter independence, following Shimony (1986), Shimony (1990)).
For fixed values of the experimental settings, Bell’s Principle of Local Causality entails that the outcomes of the experiments on the two systems be independent, conditional on the specification \(z\) of the complete state of the system at the source. This is the outcome independence condition.
(OI) For each pair of parameter settings \(a,b\), and all \(z\), and all \(s \in S_a\) and \(\tau \in T_b\),
\[p_{a,b}(s,\tau \mid z) = p^1_{a,b}(s \mid z)\; p^2_{a,b}(\tau \mid z). \tag{3.19}\]
A violation of PI would seem to permit superluminal signalling, but this requires an additional assumption: that the state of the system be controllable. It would not hold for a theory on which there are principled limitations on the ability of would-be signallers to control the states of the systems they are dealing with; an example of a theory of this sort is Bohmian mechanics, which violates PI but does not permit superluminal signalling. In some of the literature, PI has incorrectly been treated as equivalent to no-signalling.


3.1.3 Explicit experimental assumptions

3.1.3.1 Unique experimental outcomes
Of the potential outcomes of a given experiment, one and only one occurs, and hence it makes sense to speak of the outcome of an experiment. However, Everettian, or “many-worlds”, interpretations state that all potential outcomes actually occur. Even in these interpretations, though, each individual world has a unique outcome.


3.1.3.2 Experimental settings as free parameters
It is assumed that the complete state \(z\) is always sampled from the same probability distribution \(\delta\), no matter what choice of experiment is made, and that, for this reason, the subset of experiments corresponding to any given choice of settings is a fair sample of the distribution of \(z\). This will be discussed in more detail in Bell’s theorem and metaphysics.


3.1.3.3 Timing of experimental outcomes
In experiments, care should be taken that, for the two subsystems, the choice of experimental setting and the registration of results take place at spacelike separation. It is assumed that experiments have unique results. The question arises as to when the unique result emerges. It is typically assumed that the result is definite once a detector has been triggered or the result has been recorded in a computer memory. This difficulty will remain unresolved until the quantum mechanical measurement problem is solved.

section: 3.2 Appendix: quantum mechanical calculation of the CHSH inequality
text:
3.2 Appendix: quantum mechanical calculation of the CHSH inequality
The joint measurement probabilities of two entangled photons are calculated, their correlation function is found, and it is shown how they violate the limits of classical physics.

3.2.1 1. The initial entangled state
In an optical setup using spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC), a pair of photons are generated and sent to measurement equipment \(A\) and \(B\) in a maximally entangled polarisation state described by the symmetric Bell state, Equation 3.13-:
\[\Phi = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\phi_{\chi,1} \otimes \phi_{\chi, 2} + \phi_{\upsilon, 1} \otimes\phi_{\upsilon, 2} \right),\]
Here, \(\phi_{\chi}\) and \(\phi_{\upsilon}\) represent horizontal and vertical linear polarisations. This state means that if settings \(a\) at \(A\) and \(b\) at \(B\) both measure in the \(\chi\) or \(\upsilon\) direction, they will always get identical results (either both \(\chi\) or both \(\upsilon\)).


3.2.2 2. The measurement bases
Settings \(a\) and \(b\) can be independently rotated.

the \(a\) setting of polariser I is the angle \(\alpha\);
the \(b\) setting of polariser II is the angle \(\beta\).

A polariser at angle \(\theta\) measures whether a photon is polarised along that angle (\(+1\) result) or perpendicular to it (\(-1\) result). Write these measurement states as:
\[\psi_{+\theta} = \cos\theta \phi_{\chi} + \sin\theta \phi_{\upsilon}\]
\[\psi_{-\theta} = -\sin\theta \phi_{\chi} + \cos\theta \phi_{\upsilon}\]


3.2.3 3. Calculating joint probabilities
Require the probability that the settings \(a\) and \(b\) both detect a photon passing through their polarisers (\(+1,+1\)). According to Born’s rule, this is the squared magnitude of the inner product of the measurement state and the initial state:
\[p_{++}(\alpha, \beta) = |(\psi_{+\alpha} \otimes \psi_{+\beta}, \Phi)|^2\]
First, let us find the inner product:
\[(\psi_{+\alpha} \otimes \psi_{+\beta}, \Phi)\] \[ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left(
     \left( \phi_{\chi,1} \cos\alpha + \phi_{\upsilon,1} \sin\alpha \right) \otimes \left( \phi_{\chi,2} \cos\beta + \phi_{\upsilon,2} \sin\beta \right) , \left( \phi_{\chi,1} \otimes \phi_{\chi,2} + \phi_{\upsilon,1} \otimes \phi_{\upsilon,2} \right) \right)\]
Because \((\phi_{\chi}, \phi_{\chi}) = 1\) and \((\phi_{\chi}, \phi_{\upsilon}) = 0\), this simplifies to:
\[\left(\psi_{+\alpha} \otimes \psi_{+\beta}, \Phi\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (\cos\alpha \cos\beta + \sin\alpha \sin\beta)\]
Using the trigonometric identity \(\cos(\alpha - \beta) = \cos\alpha \cos\beta + \sin\alpha \sin\beta\),
\[\left(\psi_{+\alpha} \otimes \psi_{+\beta}, \Phi\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cos(\alpha - \beta)\]
Squaring this gives the joint probability of both getting \(+1\):
\[p_{++}(\alpha, \beta) = \frac{1}{2} \cos^2(\alpha - \beta)\]
By doing the same for the other combinations (for example, using \(\phi_{-\alpha}\) or \(\phi_{-\beta}\)), the full set of joint probabilities is:

\(p_{++}\) (both pass): \(\frac{1}{2} \cos^2(\alpha - \beta)\)
\(p_{--}\) (both blocked): \(\frac{1}{2} \cos^2(\alpha - \beta)\)
\(p_{+-}\) (\(a\) passes, \(b\) blocked): \(\frac{1}{2} \sin^2(\alpha - \beta)\)
\(p_{-+}\) (\(a\) blocked, \(b\) passes): \(\frac{1}{2} \sin^2(\alpha - \beta)\)



3.2.4 4. The expectation value (correlation function)
The correlation function \(E(\alpha, \beta)\) is the average product of their measurement outcomes. Weighting the matching results (\(+1 \times +1 = 1\) and \(-1 \times -1 = 1\)) positively, and the opposing results (\(+1 \times -1 = -1\)) negatively:
\[E(\alpha, \beta) = p_{++} + p_{--} - p_{+-} - p_{-+}\]
Substituting the probabilities just calculated:
\[E(\alpha, \beta) = \left( \frac{1}{2} \cos^2(\alpha - \beta) + \frac{1}{2} \cos^2(\alpha - \beta) \right) - \left( \frac{1}{2} \sin^2(\alpha - \beta) + \frac{1}{2} \sin^2(\alpha - \beta) \right)\]
\[E(\alpha, \beta) = \cos^2(\alpha - \beta) - \sin^2(\alpha - \beta)\]
Using the identity \(\cos(2\theta) = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta\), the quantum correlation function is derived as:
\[E(\alpha, \beta) = \cos(2(\alpha - \beta))\]
This is exactly the result as stated in Equation 3.14, with \(\alpha-\beta = \theta_{ab}\), confirming that the quantum mechanical predictions for the correlation function violate the CHSH inequality for certain choices of angles \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).

title: 4  Possibilist Transactional Quantum Theory (PTQT)
text:
4.1 The quantum substratum
Ruth Kastner’s “Relativistic (Possibilist) Transactional Interpretation” (PTI) gives a very explicit and technically different answer to Bell locality than Cramer’s original Transactional Interpretation (TI). Her answer is grounded in direct‑action quantum field theory (DAQFT) and an ontology of real physical possibilities leading to spacetime events.
This chapter presents a concise conceptual summary of Possibilist Transactional Quantum Theory (PTQT), focusing on two questions:
To address the first point, a simple change will be made. All talk of waves will be eliminated. The immewdiate changes are:
Kastner’s PTI is often described as an interpretation of quantum mechanics (Kastner (2022)). In this chapter, it is treated as a physical theory with explicit ontological commitments; for that reason, the name Possibilist Transactional Quantum Theory (PTQT) is used to reflect this status.
The core claim is that a quantum substratum of physically real possibilities underlies, and specifically causes, observable spacetime events. The theory addresses both the measurement problem and Bell-type correlations. Except for the ad hoc measurement step in standard quantum theory all quantum processes take place in the substratum. They are not spacetime processes. In PTQT, the substratum is a domain of potentiality rather than a collection of actual spacetime objects. It is not directly observable; its structure is inferred from the formalism and from the pattern of actualized events.

If time in the empirical sense is emergent then what is it that indexes the dynamics in the pre-spacetime quantum substrate? In the PTQT spacetime is not a fundamental container. Instead, physical spacetime and its temporal structure emerge from a deeper, extra-spatiotemporal realm called the quantum substratum (Kastner (2022)). The time mechanism in this framework operates through the following core concepts:

In PTQT, the quantum substratum consists of quantum states existing as potentiae (possibilities or unactualized offers and responses). Time does not flow smoothly as a background parameter in this substratum. Rather, spacetime events and their structural connections are established exclusively by “actualized transactions”.

When a quantum emitter sends an offer wave and an absorber responds, a transaction can become actualized (a process corresponding to objective wave function collapse).
An actualized transaction instantiates a discrete emission event, an absorption event, and the invariant spacetime interval connecting them. Spacetime effectively “crystallizes” out of these events.

PTQT rejects the “block universe” ontology where past, present, and future all exist simultaneously.

In the quantum substratum, the primary temporal feature is ontological change driven by the state transitions of interacting quantum systems.
The “Now” is the shifting domain of active actualization. The future does not exist yet because it consists only of unactualized possibilities within the substratum. A time index (\(t\)) is merely a relational way of indexing and mapping these changes after they have been archived into the emergent fabric of spacetime.

Standard quantum mechanics operates on time-symmetric laws, making it a mystery why time only moves forward. RTI solves this by introducing a physical mechanism for temporal symmetry breaking:

The unactualized offers and responses in the substratum are fundamentally time-symmetric.
However, the non-unitary phase where an absorber responds transforms the time-symmetric propagator into the time-asymmetric Feynman propagator (which propagates positive energy forward in time).
This actualization process inherently breaks time symmetry, generating a unidirectional arrow of time and grounding the Second Law of Thermodynamics.


In summary, normal time is relational and emergent: the quantum substratum itself is extra-spatiotemporal, while the linear flow of time we perceive is a macro-level byproduct of discrete, irreversible quantum transactions breaking symmetry at the micro-level.
As the quantum substratum is extra-spatiotemporal, how can we speak of “unitary evolution” (like the solution of the Heisenberg equation or quantum operators) which explicitly depends on a time parameter? Ruth Kastner resolves this by introducing a strict distinction between two fundamentally different types of time: Coordinate Time (which is emergent and relational) and Process Time (which is fundamental and non-spatial). Here is how unitary dynamics can function in a substratum without relying on physical spacetime:

4.2.1 Process Time vs. Coordinate Time
In PTQT, the time parameter (t) found in standard quantum mechanical equations does not refer to the ticking of a clock in physical space. Instead, it refers to Process Time:

Process Time: This is a sequential, logical ordering of changes in quantum states. It represents the generation of possibilities—offers being sent and responses being generated. It is a time of becoming, not a time of extension.
Coordinate Time: This is the time we measure with macro-clocks (e.g., \(x^0\) in relativity). It only exists after a transaction has collapsed the quantum state and created a physical event.

Therefore, unitary dynamics describes the evolution of possibilities in Process Time before they ever “solidify” into the Coordinate Time of our physical universe. Because the substratum lacks spatial distance, all quantum systems within it are fundamentally in a state of immediate, non-local availability to one another.Therefore: - Unitary evolution in this realm is not a movement through space over time. The time \(t\) in the unitary operator \(U(t)=e^{-iHt}\) acts as a relational index for these internal state changes, rather than a measure of duration through an external physical container.

In axiomatic foundation for quantum theory as proposed in Haag (1996), Haag locality is a spacetime concept, and PTQT denies that spacetime is fundamental. Local operator algebras assigned to spacetime regions

Microcausality: operators in spacelike‑separated regions commute

Haag duality: the algebra of a region equals the commutant of its causal complement

All of these pillars require:

A background spacetime

A causal structure

Localizable observables

Region‑indexed operator algebras

4.8 State preparation, spacetime and the quantum substratum”
State preparation has similarities with measurement. A measurement leaves the system under investigation in a certain state. State preparation in Kastner’s Relativistic Transactional Interpretation (PTQT) (Kastner (2022)) influences the quantum substratum by selecting and shaping the set of incipient transactions that exist as physically real possibilities prior to spacetime actualisation. It does so through isolating the system under investigation and then controlling its interactions with a preparatory absorber.
The setting up of the preparatory absorber takes place in spacetime, but the state preparation is not in spacetime; it is a constraint on the pre‑spacetime possibility structure from which actualised events emerge.
In PTQT, state preparation modifies the quantum substratum by altering the configuration of emission states of the system under investigation and absorber states that exist as pre‑spacetime possibilities. These prepared states determine which incipient transactions are available and therefore which spacetime events can emerge through the non‑unitary (NU) actualisation process.
Kastner describes the quantum substratum as a pre‑spacetime domain consisting of quantum systems with rest mass and internal periodicities that act as “internal clocks” and define inertial frames. The substratum contains in Kastner’s terminology:

Offer waves (OWs) generated by emitters

Confirmation waves (CWs) generated by absorbers

Incipient transactions: matched OW–CW pairs representing possible energy‑transferring events

These are representations of possibilities in Hilbert space.
The generalised probability reconstructions of quantum mechanics and now the enhanced PTQT show that the quantum substratum is a pre‑spacetime domain in which the possibilities for actualisation are constrained by the global structure of the system. State preparation is a process that constrains the substratum and thereby influences which spacetime events can emerge. There is no place other than historical respect for Schrodinger to talk about waves. So instead of describing the processes in terms of offer waves and confirmation waves, we can describe them in terms of the emission states (ES) of the system under investigation and the absorber states (AS).
State preparation—whether by measurement, filtering, or controlled interactions—changes the quantum state that undergoes unitary evolution (the U‑interaction).
Prepared states determine:

which ES exist,
their amplitudes,
their phase relations,
the set of potential absorbers,
and therefore the structure of incipient transactions.

Thus, state preparation reconfigures the landscape of possibilities in the substratum.

4.8.1 How state preparation influences the substratum
It changes the set of emission states by preparing a quantum state, which changes the ES of a system. Since ES are the “invitations to transact,” modifying them directly alters the substratum’s possibility structure. It changes which absorber states can respond to the emission states, and therefore which incipient transactions can form. Absorbers respond only to ES components compatible with their coupling.
State preparation can: - suppress certain components (e.g., filtering out momentum modes), - enhance others, - or entangle systems so that absorber states reflect joint absorber behaviour.
It changes the pattern of incipient transactions by forming them wherever ES–AS matches occur. State preparation determines:

which matches are possible,

their relative weights,

their global constraints (especially in entangled systems).

This is crucial because actualisation selects one incipient transaction via what Kastner calls spontaneous symmetry breaking. There is no explanatory mechanism for this “symmetry breaking” in PTQT, but the selection of the actual outcome is more analogous to random sampling. But there is no sampling mechanism. All there is, is a dispositional weighted set of tendencies for each possibletransaction and a stochastically selected outcome.

Because state preparation determines the set of incipient transactions, it also determines:

the correlations that can appear,
the global constraints on entangled systems,
and the structure of possible actualisations.

This is why PTQT can explain Bell correlations without spacetime nonlocality:
the correlations arise from global constraints in the substratum, not from signals between spacetime events.

title: 5  Conclusion
text:
5.1 Summary of the Argument
This book set out to reconstruct quantum mechanics on a probabilistic footing, using the \(\sigma\)-complex formalism of Chapter 1, and then to ask what this reconstruction implies for locality. Three distinct notions of locality have been distinguished:
The central tension explored is that microcausality and Haag locality both presuppose a fixed spacetime background, while the violation of Bell locality shows that entangled systems are correlated in a way no local common cause can explain. Standard quantum mechanics accommodates this by remaining silent on the mechanism connecting preparation and measurement outcomes, deferring to the Born rule and to an unanalyzed notion of measurement.
The relational/probabilistic reconstruction developed here, together with the discussion of Possibilist Transactional Quantum Theory (PTQT) as an explicit ontological proposal, offers an alternative: entanglement and nonlocal correlation are located not in spacetime but in a pre-spacetime quantum substratum of physical possibilities, from which spacetime events emerge through the actualisation of transactions. On this view, Bell nonlocality is not a violation of causal locality, because the correlations do not require any propagating spacetime influence; and Haag locality, being a spacetime-dependent axiom, cannot be treated as fundamental if the substratum picture is correct.

title: 5  Conclusion
text:
Causal locality (microcausality): the requirement, inherited from special and general relativity, that operators associated with spacelike-separated regions commute (Section 2.1).
Bell locality: the statistical independence assumption used in the derivation of the Bell/CHSH inequalities, whose violation by quantum mechanical predictions is confirmed by experiment (Chapter 3).
Haag locality: the axiomatic requirement of local quantum field theory that observables be assigned to spacetime regions, together with microcausality and Haag duality (Section 4.7).

title: 5  Conclusion
text:
5.2 What Has Not Been Resolved
This account is deliberately partial. Several difficulties have been identified rather than settled:

The reconstruction in terms of \(\sigma\)-complexes and conditional states clarifies the mathematics of state reduction but does not by itself supply a dynamical mechanism for reduction; the treatment of the measurement problem shows what such a mechanism must do, not what it is.
The relationship between PTQT and Haag’s axiomatic local quantum physics is one of tension rather than reconciliation: the two frameworks answer different questions about locality, and no unified formalism has been presented that recovers Haag’s local algebras as an emergent, approximate description of the substratum.
The status of the quantum substratum itself — whether it should be understood as a further physical domain requiring its own dynamics, or as a heuristic device for speaking about unmeasured possibilities — has been described rather than derived from independent principles.

title: 5  Conclusion
text:
5.3 Open Questions
The discussion points toward several questions for further work:

Can the emergence of Haag-local spacetime algebras from a pre-spacetime substratum be given a precise mathematical treatment, rather than a conceptual one?
What experimental signatures, if any, would distinguish PTQT-type substratum theories from other interpretations (Bohmian mechanics, many-worlds, relational quantum mechanics) that also reproduce the Bell-violating statistics of standard quantum mechanics?
Does the probabilistic reconstruction extend cleanly to relativistic quantum field theory, where Haag’s framework is best established, or does it require modification at that level?

These questions are not resolved here. The aim of this book has been to make the locality problem in quantum mechanics precise enough that such questions can be posed sharply, and to show that at least one substratum-based account offers a coherent, if incomplete, response to it.
